findings.title: Subset-evaluable tick and full-population neighbor visibility match the architecture
findings.description: `build()` takes the full population, and only active agents are queried and integrated. This matches the "Subset-evaluable tick" principle and the multi-resolution consideration in `100-arch.behavior-engine.md`. The caller decides which agents to evaluate, and the engine does not. The success criteria and walkthrough step 5 cover it. Dependency direction is also correct: the engine depends on the `SpatialQuery` protocol, and nothing flows back.

findings.title: The tick design contradicts the "no per-agent Python loops" requirement
findings.description:
- Step 3 calls `query_radius(position, radius)` once per active agent. That is a Python-level per-agent loop in the hot path.
- `BulkForce` receives `neighbor_lists: list[NDArray]` and `profiles: list[BehavioralProfile]`. Both are per-agent Python collections.
- The Technical Requirements say "No Python-level per-agent loops in the hot path".
- The architecture asks for "bulk array-in/array-out operations with no Python-level per-agent branching… no callbacks into Python" so that GPU offload stays possible.
- As designed, the tick fails its own requirement and the architecture's GPU-compatibility constraint.
- Either add a bulk query shape (positions array in, CSR-style flat neighbor indices plus offsets out) and pass profile parameters as per-agent arrays gathered via `profile_indices`, or explicitly scope the requirement to "force and integration math only" and record the per-agent query as accepted debt.
- The doc also never says how per-agent `max_speed` and `query_radius` are gathered into arrays for the vectorized clamp.

findings.title: The scale NFR is not restated, and the brute-force design is inconsistent with it
findings.description:
- The architecture sets "tens of thousands of agents at full behavioral fidelity on a single CPU process".
- The slice targets only "hundreds of agents" and gives no latency or agent-count target for tick.
- Determinism is restated, but the efficiency NFR is not, even though this slice builds the tick path.
- The brute-force description says `build()` computes all pairwise distances. That is an N×N matrix, about 800 MB at 10K agents in float64, and the doc calls it O(n²) on build while claiming O(n) per query.
- `query_radius` takes a *position*, not an agent index. A precomputed pairwise matrix keyed by agent index cannot answer it, so the description is incoherent.
- Fix by stating an explicit target for this slice (for example, N agents and a tick budget on the reference machine, with "tens of thousands" as the architecture's target for slice 105). Describe brute force as storing positions and computing distances on query.

findings.title: Inactive-agent handling contradicts itself between the Force Protocol and Integration sections
findings.description:
- `BulkForce` returns a full-population N×2 array, and the doc says integration will "add force to velocity for all, but only active agents have non-zero forces".
- Integration and the Data Flow say integration applies only to active agents via fancy indexing, and inactive state is untouched.
- Applying integration to all agents would still do `position += velocity * dt` for inactive agents that have nonzero velocity. That breaks the "inactive agents unchanged" success criterion.
- A full-N×2 return per force per tick also allocates O(N) even when the subset is 1/16 of the population. That undercuts the subset interface's purpose.
- The doc does not say whether `neighbor_lists` and `profiles` are indexed by position in `active_indices` or by agent index.
- Pick one contract. The simplest is for forces to return an `(len(active), DIMS)` array aligned with `active_indices`, with all per-agent inputs aligned the same way.

findings.title: `Force` protocol has no consumer in `tick()` and is speculative scope
findings.description:
- `tick()` accepts only `list[BulkForce]`. The text says "the tick loop prefers the bulk variant when available", which implies dispatch on both types that the signature does not support.
- A per-agent `Force` protocol "for testing, reference implementations" would need an adapter to run in the tick. The doc does not specify one.
- Success criteria require placeholder forces to "exercise both protocol paths", which forces the adapter and dispatch into scope.
- The architecture sanctions `BulkForce`, not a second per-agent protocol.
- Cut the `Force` protocol and its tests, or defer it until a slice needs a per-agent reference implementation. If kept, specify the adapter and the dispatch rule.
- Other items with no consumer in this slice:
  - The `accelerations` array (line 96) is never read or written by the integration formula, and the architecture's state list omits it.
  - The `DIMS` constant (lines 102, 120) is a 3D-readiness abstraction that nothing needs yet. It also does not make 3D a "single-point change" while the `NDArray[np.float64]  # 2D force vector` comments and per-force math remain.

findings.title: `SpatialQuery` contract is under-specified for slice 105's regression guarantee
findings.description:
- The slice plan says slice 105 must show "behavioral output is identical before and after the swap".
- The protocol does not say whether the querying agent is included in its own results, whether the radius boundary is inclusive, or whether returned indices are in a canonical order.
- Floating-point force summation depends on neighbor order, so an unspecified order can break bit-identical determinism when the spatial hash replaces brute force.
- Self-inclusion will force every force in 101–104 to handle it independently, and they may handle it inconsistently.
- State all three points in the protocol docstring (for example: excludes self, inclusive boundary, ascending index order), and add a test that asserts them.

findings.title: `tick()` input validation and failure behavior are not specified
findings.description:
This is an in-process API with no I/O, but the following bad inputs have no stated handling, despite the project's fail-fast rule:
- `active_indices` with out-of-range or duplicate entries. With NumPy fancy indexing, `arr[idx] += x` with duplicates silently applies the update once and gives wrong results with no error.
- `profile_indices` that point outside `profiles`.
- `dt <= 0`.
- A force whose output shape does not match.
- A zero or invalid `max_speed` in the clamp.
- An empty `active_indices`.

Specify that these raise explicit errors at the `tick()` boundary, and add tests for them.

findings.title: Add/remove semantics do not address index stability
findings.description:
- The architecture's narrow interface includes "register/remove agents".
- The world server will hold `active_indices` arrays across ticks.
- The doc says add/remove "resize arrays" but does not say whether removal compacts, swap-removes, or preserves indices, or how callers keep a stable agent identity.
- Compaction or swap-remove silently invalidates any cached index array.
- State the removal semantics and what stable identifier, if any, callers should use. The world-server contract depends on it.

findings.title: The architecture's tick contract includes an environmental context and a returned state, and the slice has neither
findings.description:
- The architecture describes the tick as receiving "environmental context" and "returning the updated state array".
- The slice's `tick()` has no environment parameter and returns `None`, mutating in place. The slice's own Technical Scope says "return updated state", so the doc contradicts itself.
- Omitting environment is reasonable, because the Environment Layer initiative is not yet defined. Say so explicitly, along with how a later environment input will be added (a new optional parameter or a force-side closure). Otherwise the claim that behavioral slices "don't modify the tick loop" is untested.
- Note the in-place mutation as a deliberate deviation from the architecture's "get back state".

findings.title: Markdown formatting defect in the Integration section
findings.description: The "Integration: Semi-Implicit Euler" heading and its content are indented four spaces. They will render as a code block instead of a heading and prose.
